title: Ransom Note
description: Brute force to optimized: searching and removing letters versus counting once and subtracting.

blocks.text: Given two strings ransomNote and magazine, return true if ransomNote can be constructed entirely using letters cut out from magazine, where each letter in magazine can only be used once.

blocks.caption: Count magazine's letters once, then subtract while scanning ransomNote

blocks.text: Given two strings ransomNote and magazine, return true if ransomNote can be constructed entirely using letters cut out from magazine, where each letter in magazine can only be used once.

blocks.title: Analogy: Cutting Letters Out of a Magazine to Spell a Message
blocks.text: Like the classic ransom note trope of cutting individual letters out of a magazine to spell a message, where every letter used must physically come from somewhere in the magazine, and once a letter is cut out, it cannot be reused for a second spot.

blocks.caption: Every letter needed in the note must be available in the magazine, without reusing any letter twice

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The magazine has no letter \"a\" at all","the note cannot be built","Every letter used in ransomNote must physically be available in magazine; \"a\" simply is not present"],["Answer","false","At least one required letter is completely unavailable"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The magazine has exactly two \"a\" letters available","enough to build the note","ransomNote needs exactly two \"a\" letters, and magazine supplies exactly that many"],["Answer","true","Every letter ransomNote needs is available in sufficient quantity"]]}

blocks.text: The magazine only has one "a" available, but the note needs two, so the answer is false.

Before searching through magazine for each letter, notice that the real question being asked, over and over, is always the same shape: "is there still one more of this specific letter available", which is a counting question, not a searching question.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Whether ransomNote can be built depends entirely on quantities, how many of each letter magazine offers versus how many of each letter ransomNote needs, never on the order the letters appear in.

Observation 2: Searching through a live, shrinking copy of magazine for each character of ransomNote answers the right question, but does it the slow way, by scanning instead of by direct lookup.

Observation 3: If the count of every letter in magazine is tallied once up front, then checking whether ransomNote can be built becomes simply subtracting 1 from the relevant count for every character of ransomNote and checking that no count would ever need to go below 0.

Observation 4: Since only lowercase English letters are involved, a plain 26 element array indexed by letter is enough to hold every count, no hash map overhead required.

Whenever a problem is really about "do I have enough of each item," count everything once up front, then consume from those counts directly, instead of repeatedly searching a shrinking collection.

This is one of the most common hash-table (or fixed-array) patterns in interviews: precompute frequencies once, then answer many consumption or comparison questions against those frequencies in constant time each.
For every character needed in ransomNote, search through a working copy of the magazine's letters to find and remove one matching letter.

items: Convert magazine into a mutable list of letters.
For every character in ransomNote, search that list for a matching letter and remove it if found.
If any character cannot be found, the note cannot be built.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: magazine is converted into a mutable list, ArrayList, or vector up front, since the original string type in each language does not support efficient in-place removal of a single matched character.
available.remove(ch) removes only one matching occurrence, not every occurrence, since only one instance of a letter should be consumed per character of ransomNote.

The function returns false immediately the moment any character of ransomNote cannot be found, rather than finishing the scan first, since no later successful match can undo an already-missing letter.

blocks.text: Every letter needed by ransomNote is matched against an actually available letter in magazine, removed once used, so this correctly enforces the "used only once" rule.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times m), searching and removing from the available list for every character of ransomNote.
Space: O(m), for the mutable copy of magazine's letters.

Limitation: searching linearly through the remaining letters for every single character of ransomNote is far slower than necessary, when the total count of each letter available could instead be tracked directly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's real cost is repeating the same kind of search, "find one instance of this letter among what remains", once per character of ransomNote, and each search scans through however many letters are still left in the shrinking magazine copy. But nothing about that search actually needs the letters' positions or order, only how many of each are left. Precomputing the total count of every letter in magazine once replaces every one of those repeated scans with a single array lookup and decrement. The only extra care needed is checking that a count does not go negative, which is exactly the moment a letter has been fully used up, matching the point where the brute force's search would have failed to find anything left.

Count how many times each letter appears in magazine using a fixed size array or hash map. Then, for every character needed in ransomNote, decrement its available count; if any count would go negative, the note cannot be built.
Count every letter in magazine once, then subtract counts while scanning ransomNote.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Count magazine letters","a: 2, b: 1","Tallying once up front captures exactly how many of each letter is available before any consumption happens"],["Subtract for the first \"a\" in ransomNote","a: 1","One instance of \"a\" has now been used, leaving one fewer available for the rest of ransomNote"],["Subtract for the second \"a\" in ransomNote","a: 0, still valid","The count reaching exactly 0, not going negative, means this letter was used exactly as many times as it was available"],["Every character of ransomNote was covered without going negative","true","No letter was ever needed more times than it was available, so ransomNote can be fully constructed"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: count magazine letters once, then subtract as ransomNote is scanned

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n plus m), one pass over each string.
Space: O(1), since the alphabet is fixed size.

Counting every letter in magazine once captures the exact total supply of each letter, and decrementing that count once per matching character in ransomNote precisely simulates "using up" one physical letter, since each decrement corresponds to consuming exactly one occurrence. A count reaching exactly 0 exactly matches supply meeting demand exactly; a count that would go negative means ransomNote demanded one more of that letter than magazine could ever supply, which is exactly when the answer must be false.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation for a given letter","Meaning"],"rows":[["Count is greater than 0 when needed","Enough of this letter remains; consume one and continue"],["Count is already 0 when needed","This letter is fully exhausted; ransomNote cannot be built"]]}

items: counts[ch - 'a'] (or the dict/hash-map equivalent) maps each lowercase letter directly to its own slot, since 'a' through 'z' map cleanly onto indices 0 through 25.
The first loop tallies magazine's letters completely before the second loop begins, so every count reflects magazine's full, true supply before any of it is consumed.
Checking whether a letter's count is already 0 happens before decrementing, so a letter's count is never allowed to go below 0.
The second loop's decrement happens only after confirming availability, keeping the counts array an accurate "remaining supply" at every step.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (search and remove)","O(n times m)","O(m)","Every character of ransomNote triggers a linear search through the shrinking magazine copy"],["Optimized (count once, then subtract)","O(n plus m)","O(1)","One pass to tally magazine, one pass to consume from ransomNote, using a fixed 26-slot array"]]}

blocks.text: This is another instance of the character frequency counting pattern: counting availability once and decrementing as it is consumed replaces repeated linear searches with constant time lookups.

items: Removing a matched letter from a live copy of magazine using linear search, instead of just decrementing a count, which reintroduces the same inefficiency the optimized approach is meant to avoid.
Forgetting that ransomNote could require more of a letter than magazine has available, and needing to fail correctly the moment that happens rather than only checking after fully scanning ransomNote.
Using a general hash map when a fixed 26 element array would do, adding unnecessary hashing overhead for a problem that guarantees only lowercase English letters.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["An empty ransomNote","Trivially always constructible regardless of magazine, since there are no letters left to check"],["ransomNote longer than magazine","Can immediately be rejected, since there simply are not enough letters available in total no matter their arrangement"]]}

items: Mention that a fixed size 26 element array is sufficient and slightly faster than a general hash map here, since the problem guarantees only lowercase English letters.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Can string A be built from the characters of string B, each used at most once" points toward frequency counting: count B's characters once, then consume from those counts while scanning A, failing the moment a needed character runs out.

items: What if magazine could be reused across many different ransomNote checks? Precompute magazine's counts once outside the function, and only re-copy or reset counts per query, avoiding recounting magazine every single time.

What if the alphabet included uppercase letters or digits too? A plain 26 element array no longer covers every character; either widen the array's size to cover the full relevant character set or fall back to a general hash map.

How would you handle Unicode characters instead of a small fixed alphabet? A fixed size array indexed directly by character code is no longer practical; a hash map keyed by character remains the right structure regardless of alphabet size.
Same frequency counting pattern as Valid Anagram and Group Anagrams, just applied to a "does A fit within B's supply" question instead of an exact-match or grouping question.
Same "count once, then consume and check for exhaustion" technique used in Word Pattern and Contains Duplicate style problems that also need frequency, not just presence, information.
Same "a small fixed alphabet array beats a general hash map" efficiency insight seen throughout string and bit manipulation problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n times m) time, O(m) space.
Optimized: O(n plus m) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Frequency counting with consume-and-check-exhaustion
Core Idea: Count every letter magazine supplies once, then subtract one per character ransomNote demands, failing the instant a letter's supply runs out
Time: O(n plus m)
Space: O(1), a fixed 26-element array regardless of input size
Most Important Observation: A "do I have enough of each item" question is a counting problem, not a searching problem, once frequencies are precomputed
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Count the magazine once, spend from it like a budget
